stem: A nightly `dbt build` fails partway through. The on-call engineer wants two genuinely useful, documented ways to control how a pipeline reacts to failures, without changing what each individual test actually checks. Which TWO are real, documented levers?

option_texts.A: Pass `--fail-fast` so dbt exits immediately on the first failure instead of continuing to run unrelated models
option_texts.B: Set `on_error: continue` on a model so its downstream models can still run even when that model fails
option_texts.C: Set every test's severity to `warn` across the board, since that is the only way to stop a failure from skipping anything
option_texts.D: Increase `--threads` to a very high number, since more concurrency automatically prevents cascading skips

drill_answer_short: --fail-fast and on_error: continue both control failure handling without changing what a test checks
decision_hinge: Supply the -x or --fail-fast flag to dbt run, dbt build, or dbt test to make dbt exit immediately on the first failure. Set on_error: continue on a model to allow its downstream models to run even when that model fails.

plausible_options.C: wants two genuinely useful, documented ways to control how a pipeline reacts to failures

eliminated_by.D: without changing what each individual test actually checks

distractor_traps.C: T8: scope error — severity: warn is a real lever, but it changes what the test reports, and it is not the only way to control skipping
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — thread count has no documented effect on skip propagation

stem: Under `dbt build`, `model_b` depends on `model_a`. A `unique` test on `model_a` fails. The release engineer needs to know exactly what happens to `model_b`. What's the outcome?

option_texts.A: `model_b` builds but is flagged with a warning in the run results
option_texts.B: `model_b` still builds normally, because only a test failed, not the model itself
option_texts.C: `model_b` is skipped entirely, because a test failure on an upstream resource blocks and skips its downstream resources
option_texts.D: The entire `dbt build` invocation aborts immediately, stopping every other model too

drill_answer_short: A failing test on model_a's unique column causes model_b to skip entirely
decision_hinge: Tests on upstream resources will block downstream resources from running, and a test failure will cause those downstream resources to skip entirely. E.g. If model_b depends on model_a, and a unique test on model_a fails, then model_b will SKIP.

eliminated_by.A: The release engineer needs to know exactly what happens to `model_b`

B.requires_fact: A test failure will cause downstream resources to skip entirely; a failing test is not the same as the model itself continuing to run normally.

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — a skip is not the same as a warning tag on a successful build
distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — the documented example states this exact scenario causes a skip
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — aborting the whole invocation is --fail-fast behaviour, not the default skip rule

stem: A team wants to copy their production models into a PR's CI schema cheaply, on a platform that supports zero-copy cloning of tables. They need to know what `dbt clone` actually creates for a model that is materialized as a table in the source environment there. What does it create?

option_texts.A: Nothing; zero-copy cloning only works on views, never on tables
option_texts.B: A simple pointer view that runs `select * from` the source object, which is what happens without zero-copy cloning support
option_texts.C: A brand-new table populated by copying every row through a full `dbt build`, since no platform supports zero-copy cloning for tables
option_texts.D: A clone of the table made via the platform's native cloning feature, rather than copying all the data

drill_answer_short: On a platform with zero-copy cloning, dbt clone creates a true clone of a source table
decision_hinge: If your data platform supports zero-copy cloning of tables (Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery), and this model exists as a table in the source environment, dbt will create it in your target environment as a clone. Otherwise, dbt will create a simple pointer view.

plausible_options.B: on a platform that supports zero-copy cloning of tables

eliminated_by.A: materialized as a table in the source environment there

C.signal: wants to copy their production models into a PR's CI schema cheaply
C.requires_fact: If your data platform supports zero-copy cloning of tables and this model exists as a table in the source environment, dbt will create it in your target environment as a clone, rather than copying every row.

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — dbt clone works on tables too, exactly when zero-copy cloning is supported
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — the pointer-view fallback applies when zero-copy cloning is not supported, the opposite of this scenario
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — copying every row through a build defeats the stated goal of a cheap clone

stem: A column `status` on the `orders` model must only ever contain `'placed'`, `'shipped'`, `'completed'`, or `'returned'`. The team is on a current dbt version and wants the config written in the form the docs now recommend, not the older top-level form. How should the `accepted_values` test be configured?

option_texts.A: Set `values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'completed', 'returned']` directly as a top-level property of `accepted_values`, with no `arguments:` key
option_texts.B: Nest the allowed values under an `arguments:` key, with `values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'completed', 'returned']` inside it
option_texts.C: Use a `relationships` test instead, since `accepted_values` was renamed in a recent dbt release
option_texts.D: List the allowed values as a Python list inside the model's SQL file, not in YAML at all

drill_answer_short: Current dbt nests accepted_values arguments like 'values' under an arguments: key
decision_hinge: accepted_values: arguments: values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'completed', 'returned'] -- available in v1.10.5 and higher. Older versions can set the argument name as the top-level property.

plausible_options.A: wants the config written in the form the docs now recommend, not the older top-level form

eliminated_by.C: A column `status` on the `orders` model must only ever contain
eliminated_by.D: The team is on a current dbt version and wants the config written in the form the docs now recommend

distractor_traps.A: T6: stale behaviour — the top-level form still works as an alias, but it is the older form, not the currently recommended one
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — accepted_values was not renamed or replaced by relationships
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt data tests are configured in YAML, not inline Python lists in SQL files

stem: A team wants a reusable test that can be attached to any column on any model, checking that every value is strictly positive. They write a `{% test %}` block for it. Which two parameters must that block declare to make the test generic across models and columns?

option_texts.A: `source_name` and `column_name`, since generic tests always test a source rather than a model
option_texts.B: `table_name` and `field_name`, because those describe what the test checks in plain English
option_texts.C: `model` and `column_name`, the two arguments dbt passes into a generic test block so it can run against any model and column
option_texts.D: No parameters; dbt infers the model and column from the YAML property where the test is attached

drill_answer_short: A generic test block takes model and column_name as its two parameters
decision_hinge: A generic data test is defined in a test block, which contains a parameterized query and accepts arguments. There are two arguments, model and column_name, which are then templated into the query, making the data test generic across models and columns.

plausible_options.A: a reusable test that can be attached to any column on any model

eliminated_by.B: checking that every value is strictly positive

D.signal: They write a `{% test %}` block for it
D.requires_fact: A generic data test is defined in a test block, which contains a parameterized query and accepts arguments, with model and column_name templated into the query.

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — the argument is called model even when the test is attached to a source
distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — dbt's generic test block argument names are model and column_name, not these
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — the stem says they write a test block, which requires declared parameters

stem: Every `customer_id` value in the `orders` model must already exist as an `id` value in the `customers` model, enforcing referential integrity. Which built-in generic test checks this, and how is it configured?

option_texts.A: A custom singular test comparing `customer_id` row counts between `orders` and `customers`
option_texts.C: `unique`, because referential integrity is really just uniqueness enforced across two models
option_texts.D: `relationships`, configured with `arguments: {to: ref('customers'), field: id}` on the `customer_id` column

drill_answer_short: relationships checks that a column's values exist as a field in another referenced model
decision_hinge: relationships: each customer_id in the orders model exists as an id in the customers table, also known as referential integrity. Configured as relationships: arguments: to: ref('customers'), field: id.

eliminated_by.B: Every `customer_id` value in the `orders` model must already exist as an `id` value in the `customers` model
eliminated_by.C: Every `customer_id` value in the `orders` model must already exist as an `id` value in the `customers` model

distractor_traps.A: T7: over-engineering — a built-in generic test already covers this exact check
distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — accepted_values takes a literal list of values, not a ref() to another model
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — unique only checks for duplicates within one column, it never compares across models

stem: A reviewer is checking a schema.yml file and needs to flag any test name that is not one of dbt's four built-in generic tests, shipped out of the box. Which of these is NOT one of the four?
drill_answer_short: not_empty is not one of dbt's four built-in generic tests
decision_hinge: Out of the box, dbt ships with four generic data tests already defined: unique, not_null, accepted_values, and relationships.

eliminated_by.A: needs to flag any test name that is not one of dbt's four built-in generic tests

D.signal: A reviewer is checking a schema.yml file and needs to flag any test name
D.requires_fact: dbt ships with four generic data tests already defined: unique, not_null, accepted_values, and relationships.

distractor_traps.A: T8: scope error — unique is one of the four, so it cannot be the odd one out
distractor_traps.C: T8: scope error — not_null is one of the four, so it cannot be the odd one out
distractor_traps.D: T8: scope error — accepted_values is one of the four, so it cannot be the odd one out

stem: A developer writes `tests/dim_listings_min_nights.sql` as a plain `SELECT * FROM {{ ref('dim_listings_cleansed') }} WHERE minimum_nights < 1`, with no `{% test %}` wrapper and no arguments. They need to know if this file is actually usable as a dbt test without any further wrapping. Is it usable, and why?

option_texts.A: No, because singular tests must be declared in a `data_tests:` YAML property before dbt will run them
option_texts.B: No, because every test file, singular or generic, must be wrapped in a `{% test %}...{% endtest %}` block
option_texts.C: Yes, because a singular data test is simply the SQL that returns failing records, using ref() and source() like a model, needing no test block
option_texts.D: Yes, but only if the file also defines a `model` and `column_name` argument

drill_answer_short: A singular data test is just the raw SQL that returns failing rows, no test block required
decision_hinge: The simplest way to define a data test is by writing the exact SQL that will return failing records. We call these singular data tests. Singular data tests placed in the tests directory are automatically executed when running dbt test.

plausible_options.D: with no `{% test %}` wrapper and no arguments

eliminated_by.A: They need to know if this file is actually usable as a dbt test without any further wrapping

B.signal: with no `{% test %}` wrapper and no arguments
B.requires_fact: A singular data test is simply the SQL that will return failing records, needing no test block.

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — singular tests placed in tests/ are discovered and run automatically
distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — singular tests are documented as needing no test block at all
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — model and column_name are generic-test arguments, not a singular-test requirement

stem: A platform team wants every data test in the project to store its failing rows by default, without editing each test individually, and without relying on anyone remembering to pass `--store-failures` on the command line. Where should they set this, and how?

option_texts.A: Set `on_schema_change: fail` as the default on every model, which also enables failure storage for its tests
option_texts.B: Pass `--store-failures` as a permanent alias baked into every CI job definition, since that is the only way to apply it project-wide
option_texts.C: Set `store_failures: true` inside each individual test's `.yml` property, repeated for every test
option_texts.D: Under `data_tests: +store_failures: true` in `dbt_project.yml`, setting the default for all tests in the project

drill_answer_short: store_failures can be set as a project-wide default in dbt_project.yml
decision_hinge: Set the default for all tests in a package or project: dbt_project.yml data_tests: +store_failures: true.

plausible_options.B: without relying on anyone remembering to pass `--store-failures` on the command line

eliminated_by.A: store its failing rows by default

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — on_schema_change has no effect on test failure storage
distractor_traps.B: T7: over-engineering — a project-level config already does this without any CI job changes
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated requirement — the stem explicitly rules out editing each test individually

stem: A test is configured with `severity: warn` and a custom `error_if: '> 10'`. The team needs to know exactly how dbt evaluates this test when it returns 15 failing rows. What happens?

option_texts.A: dbt checks `error_if` first since it is explicitly configured, sees 15 > 10, and returns an error despite `severity: warn`
option_texts.B: dbt skips the `error_if` condition entirely because severity is `warn`, and jumps straight to evaluating `warn_if` instead
option_texts.C: dbt ignores both `error_if` and `warn_if` whenever severity is `warn`, and the test always just warns regardless of the row count
option_texts.D: dbt treats the explicit `error_if` as overriding the `severity` setting, always producing an error

drill_answer_short: With severity: warn, dbt skips error_if entirely and jumps straight to warn_if
decision_hinge: If severity: warn, dbt will skip the error_if condition entirely and jump straight to the warn_if condition (defaulted to !=0). If the warn condition is met, the test warns; if not, the test passes.

C.requires_fact: If severity: warn, dbt skips error_if entirely and jumps straight to the warn_if condition; if the warn condition is met, the test warns.

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — an explicit error_if is only checked first when severity is error, not warn
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — warn_if is still evaluated under severity: warn, only error_if is skipped
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — severity is not overridden by the presence of an explicit error_if

stem: A developer writes a one-off singular test as a `.sql` file and wants `dbt test` to discover and run it automatically, without listing it anywhere else. Where must that file live in the project?

option_texts.A: In the `models/` directory, right next to the model it tests
option_texts.B: In the `macros/` directory, alongside custom generic test macros
option_texts.C: In the `tests/` directory, as defined by the project's `test-paths` config
option_texts.D: Anywhere in the project; dbt scans every directory for `.sql` files containing a `select` statement

drill_answer_short: Singular tests live in the tests/ directory, defined by test-paths, and are auto-discovered
decision_hinge: Singular data tests are defined in .sql files, typically in your tests directory, as defined by your test-paths config. Singular data tests placed in the tests directory are automatically executed when running dbt test.

plausible_options.B: writes a one-off singular test as a `.sql` file

eliminated_by.A: wants `dbt test` to discover and run it automatically, without listing it anywhere else

D.requires_fact: Singular data tests are defined in .sql files, typically in your tests directory, as defined by your test-paths config.

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — dbt does not discover tests by proximity to the model file
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — macros/ is where custom generic test definitions live, not singular test files
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — discovery is scoped to test-paths, not every project directory
